introduction: City & Guilds English is assessed across reading, writing, and speaking, listening and communicating. This tab is CSEC Compass's own guide to the spoken side of that work: following what you hear, saying what you mean clearly, and holding your end of a conversation, a discussion or a service call. Every lesson in the three modules feeds it - the reading lessons sharpen what you listen for, and the writing lessons give the plan and the register. CSEC Compass is an independent study platform and is not affiliated with, authorized or endorsed by City & Guilds. City & Guilds® is a registered trade mark of the City and Guilds of London Institute. This is a study guide written by us, not an official document: how the spoken element of your course is run and assessed is decided by your centre and by City & Guilds, so check your teacher's current instructions as well as this guide.

tasks.title: Following what you hear, once, at the speaker's speed
tasks.explanation: Listening is the skill the other two are built on. You will practise catching the shape of what is said before the detail - what is this person asking me to do - and then the specifics: names, numbers, times and the order of steps. You will also practise the small words that change everything (before, after, unless, only) and the moment a speaker corrects themselves, where the correction is the instruction and the first version is the trap. There is no audio in this subject: the listening lessons are framed as listening strategies worked on written transcripts, and the copy says so, so that what you practise here is the strategy and not a recording.

tasks.title: Saying it clearly, in a shape the listener can follow
tasks.explanation: Speaking is preparation plus delivery. The preparation is a one-minute plan for a short talk - opening, two or three points with an example each, and a close you have written rather than improvised. The delivery is mechanical before it is confident: face the listener, aim your voice at the back of the room, let a pause mark the end of an idea instead of filling it with a sound. We rehearse aloud with a timer, because three minutes is a feel you only get by speaking it. Nothing here is a script: the prepared-talk dossier below shows how one candidate planned and rehearsed, and its words are not yours to copy.

tasks.title: Holding your end of a conversation, a discussion or a service call
tasks.explanation: Most speaking you will do is not a talk: it is a conversation with a purpose - an interview, a discussion, a complaint at a counter, a request to a supervisor. We practise the moves that keep those exchanges useful: asking an open question when you need detail, answering the question that was actually asked with one detail or reason added, disagreeing with an idea without attacking the person, bringing a quiet member of a group in, and ending with one clear ask. Where the stakes are high we also practise following up in two written lines, because a spoken agreement dissolves and a written one does not.

sampleTitle: How to prepare - the three skills, practised in writing first

sample.section: Listening practice - a transcript you can count
sample.body: Use a written transcript of any spoken instruction - a recipe read aloud, a bus announcement, a clinic's phone message - and work it in three passes. First pass: listen or read for the shape only, and write one sentence saying what the instructions are for. Second pass: list the steps in order and mark each condition word (before, after, unless, only) next to the step it governs. Third pass: mark the point where the speaker changed their mind and write the corrected version, because that is the version you follow.
tips: The correction is the instruction: 'the office - sorry, the depot - at four' means the depot.
Count the conditions, not the sentences. A transcript with three conditions and one missed condition is a failed set of instructions.
If you cannot catch a detail, practise the repair out loud: 'Sorry, could you repeat the number?'

sample.section: Speaking practice - the one-minute plan and the timed rehearsal
sample.body: Plan a two-minute talk on a topic you already know: how the school canteen could cut its queue, why your road needs a crossing, how you learned a skill at home. Write a cue card with five lines: an opening that gives the listener something concrete, three points each with one example, and a written close. Then speak it aloud with a timer, twice. The first run tells you the length; the second tells you whether the close still lands after you have lost the thread once.
tips: One point, one example. Three supported points beat eight unsupported ones.
Rehearse the first twenty seconds most: that is the part nerves own.
Write the close, do not improvise it - it is the sentence the listener keeps.

sample.section: Communicating practice - a conversation with a purpose
sample.body: Take one real situation you will face this term: asking a supervisor for a shift change, querying a bill at a counter, speaking in a group discussion. Write the three things you must not lose: the facts in order, the one ask, and the register you will use for that listener. Then rehearse it aloud with someone who will answer you back and change the script on you, because a rehearsal that goes exactly as planned has not rehearsed anything.
tips: Answer with a sentence and one detail. Yes, no and fine leave the other person carrying the conversation.
Disagree with the idea, not the person: 'I see it differently, because…'
If the stakes are high, follow up in two written lines that confirm what was agreed and by when.

marking: What good speaking, listening and communicating looks like, in our own words: the listener follows you from the first sentence; every point arrives with an example; the pause between ideas marks the seam rather than a gap; you answer the question that was asked and add one detail; you disagree with an idea without attacking the person; and you leave the other person knowing what you want next. Nothing on this tab is a mark scheme and we publish no marks or grades for this qualification - what we publish is a way of rehearsing, counting and repairing your own speaking until those habits are the ones you keep under pressure.
checklist: Plan a short talk on five lines: a concrete opening, three points with one example each, and a close written out in full.
Rehearse standing up, facing a listener, with the voice aimed at the back of the room - not at your own paper.
Time every rehearsal. Three minutes is a feel you get by speaking it, not by counting words on a page.
Record one rehearsal a week and count one fault at a time: fillers, abandoned sentences, pauses inside an idea, or eye-contact breaks.
Practise the interruption deliberately: have someone ask a question mid-point and disagree once, then rehearse the bridge sentence 'that is point 2, and I will come back to it'.
For listening, work a written transcript in three passes: the purpose, the steps with their conditions, and the point where the speaker changed their mind.
Learn the repair phrases by heart - 'Sorry, could you repeat that number?' and 'Could you say that again more slowly?' - and use them instead of guessing.
For any high-stakes conversation, write the facts in order, one clear ask, and two lines of follow-up afterwards that confirm what was agreed and by when.

categories.comment: On this dossier's own ten-point practice scale - the guide on this tab publishes no marks or grades for the qualification, and this sample claims none: the candidate worked three written transcripts each week in three counted passes and marked every condition word next to the step it governed. The count that improved most was the corrections: 2 missed in week 1, none after week 3, because the correction was written down as the instruction rather than remembered.

The talk is evidenced by counted recordings rather than by a claim: fillers 9 - 4 - 1, abandoned sentences 3 - 1 - 0, pauses inside an idea 6 - 3 - 1, and the close written in full and rehearsed last. The first timed rehearsal ran to four minutes eighteen seconds with six unsupported points; by the third recording the plan was three supported points and the run was under the candidate's own target.

The rehearsals with a listener answering back are where this section is earned: 1 of 3 interruptions answered and the plan resumed in week 5, 3 of 3 in week 6, with the seconds lost to restarting falling from 12 to 0 and the bridge sentence used three times in the final run. Every question in the last rehearsal was answered with a sentence and a detail, and the one disagreement was handled by disagreeing with the idea.

pages.heading: Method - how this talk was planned, rehearsed and repaired
pages.body:
Six weeks, eighteen short rehearsals and three recordings stand behind this dossier. The routine was the same each week: choose a topic from the candidate's own life, write a one-minute cue card, speak it aloud twice with a timer, then write down what went wrong while it was still fresh. One recording was kept each week from week 4 - three recordings in all - and a classmate answered back in the last two rehearsals so that the talk could survive being interrupted.

Everything in the method comes from the guide on this tab. Its first point is that the shape of a short talk is decided before a word is spoken, so every rehearsal began with the same five lines: a concrete opening, three points with an example each, and a written close. Its second point is that delivery is mechanical before it is confident, so the candidate rehearsed standing up, facing a listener, aiming the voice at the far wall. Its third point is that a pause marks the end of an idea, so the count that mattered was not words a minute but ideas interrupted by a sound.

The faults below were counted the day they happened, by the candidate and by the two listeners who heard the weekly run. Nothing here was written up at the end from memory, which is why the third recording sits next to the first in the tables that follow.
bullets: 18 rehearsals over 6 weeks = about 54 minutes of speech spoken aloud
3 recordings kept, one each in weeks 4, 5 and 6
Two listeners per rehearsal; a classmate answered back in the final two
Rule of the method: plan on a cue card, rehearse standing up, count the faults the same day

pages.heading: The plan - one cue card, five lines, and the topic chosen
pages.body:
The topic had to be something the candidate could speak about without research, because the talk is about fluency and organisation rather than new information: why the bus stop outside the school needs a shelter. The cue card is reproduced below as it was written - five lines, headings and a few words each, in the order they were to be spoken. The close was the only part written out in full, and it was rehearsed last so that it would be the freshest thing in the candidate's mouth.

The first version of the plan had six points and no examples, and the first timed rehearsal ran to four minutes eighteen seconds - over the length the candidate had chosen and thin on support. Two points were cut and three examples added, which is why the numbers in the results pages improve between the first and second recordings without any change to the speaking itself.

pages.heading: Results - what the three recordings counted
pages.body:
The same two listeners counted all three recordings, using the same tally sheet: an idea interrupted by a filler sound, a sentence abandoned half way, an eye-contact break longer than five seconds, and a pause that arrived in the middle of an idea rather than at its end. Counting them turned a vague feeling of 'that went badly' into three numbers that could be worked on one at a time.

The count that surprised the candidate was the filler sounds: 9 in the first recording, almost all of them at the start of a sentence, which is exactly where the plan was thinnest. Fixing the plan fixed most of the fillers, which is why the delivery count and the plan count move together below.

pages.heading: The talk - what was actually said, in order
pages.body:
What follows is the third recording, written out from the recording rather than from the plan, so the order below is the order the listener heard. The candidate's own words are kept, including the places where the spoken sentence is more relaxed than the written one would be. Reading it aloud is a useful check on your own plan: everything the listener needed was said in the first ten seconds, and the close was one sentence with one ask.

One deliberate change from the plan is visible in this version: point 2 keeps its number ('8.05') and point 3 is reduced to seven words, because the third recording was made after the candidate had cut everything that could be cut. Shorter, on this evidence, was the fix.
bullets: Opening: 'Twenty-two people, one shelter, every rainy morning. That is the queue outside our gate at 8.05.'
Point 1: wet uniform means a wet morning of lessons, and the example is the Monday in February when two classes started late.
Point 2: the queue blocks the gate, and the gate is the one the bus uses - at 8.05, the time it happens.
Point 3: one shelter against a term of missed lesson time.
Close: 'We are asking for one shelter, not a new road.'

pages.heading: Results - the two rehearsals with a listener answering back
pages.body:
The last two rehearsals were run by a classmate who was told to interrupt, ask a question in the middle and disagree once. Both were recorded and counted the same way as the solo runs, with two measures added: whether the candidate answered the interruption and returned to the plan, and whether any question produced a silence long enough to be uncomfortable.

The interruption is where a rehearsed talk usually collapses, and it is worth rehearsing deliberately: the candidate's habit was to abandon the plan and start again, which cost twelve seconds in the first booked rehearsal and cost nothing by the second. The sentence that fixed it was the short one - 'that is point 2, and I will come back to it' - which the candidate now uses as a bridge rather than a stall.

pages.heading: Discussion - what the counts exposed, and the three habits changed
pages.body:
If the numbers say one thing, it is that the talk was never a vocabulary problem. Every idea in the final recording was already in the first plan; what changed was the order they arrived in and the candidate's willingness to keep speaking while thinking. The nine fillers of recording 1 were not gaps in knowledge but gaps in the plan, and they disappeared when the plan got a fifth line rather than more words.

What worked is just as visible. Writing the close in full and rehearsing it last gave the talk somewhere to land, and the bridge sentence turned an interruption from a threat into a punctuation mark. Counting one fault at a time - fillers first, then abandoned sentences - was the only reason three recordings were enough to make the change visible.
bullets: Change 1: cut the plan to three supported points and give every point one example, because the fillers arrived where the plan had nothing to say next.
Change 2: rehearse the interruption, not just the talk - a listener who asks a question and disagrees once is a rehearsal, a silent listener is a recital.
Change 3: write the close and rehearse it last, so the sentence the listener keeps is the one sentence under control.

pages.heading: Conclusion - what this dossier shows, and what not to copy from it
pages.body:
Speaking well is a set of countable habits, not a personality. Six weeks produced 18 rehearsals, three counted recordings and one talk that survived being interrupted: fillers down from 9 to 1, abandoned sentences from 3 to 0, silences over five seconds from 2 to 0, and every question in the final rehearsal answered with a sentence and a detail.

The failures in the middle are the useful part. The first recording was too long because the plan had six points; the first interruption cost twelve seconds of restarting; the first close was improvised and wandered. None of those would have been repaired by learning more words, and all three were repaired by changing a habit.

What to copy: the five-line cue card, the timer, the counted faults, the written close and the bridge sentence for interruptions. What not to copy: this topic, these words and these numbers, which belong to one invented candidate. Your talk must be about something you can speak about without notes, in your own words.
bullets: The cue card is the method worth copying: five lines, three points, one example each
Count one fault at a time, or you will only ever see the total
The close is written, never improvised

pages.heading: What this dossier is, and what it is not
pages.body:
This is an invented dossier, written for CSEC Compass so that a student can see a finished preparation record for a short talk end to end: the plan, the counts, the words spoken, the interruptions and the two habits that survived them. The candidate, the school, the topic, the two listeners, the recordings and every count in it are invented. It is not a real candidate's work, not a record of a real assessment, and not an example published by anyone else, and nothing in it has been reproduced from any published source.

One thing worth stating plainly, because these pages contain numbers: the marks columns on the card above are this dossier's own ten-point practice scale, used to show which parts of the preparation were solid and which were not. They are not the marks or grades of any qualification, and this guide publishes none - how the spoken element of your course is run and assessed is a matter for your centre and for City & Guilds, and your teacher's current instructions are the ones that count. Read this dossier for its method and its honesty, then prepare and speak your own talk in your own words.
bullets: Invented for this sample: candidate, school, topic, listeners, recordings, counts and rehearsals
Original words: the plan, the talk, the bridge sentence and every comment in this dossier were written for CSEC Compass
Not a script: the topic, the examples and the close must come from your own life
The marks columns are a practice scale, not an official mark

examinerNotes: Listening is evidenced by counted passes over three written transcripts rather than by a claim: every condition word marked beside the step it governs, and the missed corrections falling from 2 to 0 across the six weeks.

The talk is evidenced by three recordings counted the same way by the same two listeners: 22 faults, then 10, then 3, with the filler count falling from 9 to 1 and the abandoned sentences from 3 to 0.

Communicating is evidenced by the two rehearsals with a listener answering back: interruptions answered and the plan resumed 1 of 3 then 3 of 3, seconds lost to restarting 12 then 0, and every question answered with a sentence and a detail in the final run.

The reflection is candid and quantified: it keeps the first-run counts that embarrass it (nine fillers, a four-minute talk, an improvised close) beside the counts that repaired them, and draws the honest lesson - that the problems were habits of planning and delivery rather than missing words.

Honesty: this is a sample, not a real submission. The candidate, school, topic, listeners, recordings and every count are invented for CSEC Compass, no published material is reproduced, and the marks columns are this dossier's own ten-point practice scale rather than an official mark - the guide on this tab publishes no marks or grades for the qualification, and no sample can tell you how your own centre will assess you.
